note: Produced against live testnet by scripts/, except where a block names a different producer. Every hash here is checkable in an explorer. No secret key appears in this file or anywhere in the repository; the accounts below are disposable testnet accounts.
recordedAtNote: The date of the most recent run in this file, which is what the landing page reads. Individual blocks carry their own dates where they were recorded on a different day; `walkthrough` and `denyAxisSurvey` are from 2026-08-02, `v4ChainRun` from 2026-08-05, and `browserRun` from 2026-08-06 for its first two runs and 2026-08-15 for its third.

walkthrough.contextRuleIdNote: Rule ids come from an on-chain counter, so each run of the script installs a new one. The script reads the id back out of the transaction rather than assuming it; this is the id the recorded run produced.

firstRun.note: The same four steps driven by hand before the script existed, kept because they are an independent second run on a different context rule (id 1).

liveDerivation.note: The other half of the claim, and the half the scripts do not cover: a boundary derived from a transaction that was observed on a live network rather than from a shipped fixture. Recorded here so the page that cites it reads the hash instead of restating it.
liveDerivation.producedBy: step 1 of /app/simulator, driven by hand in a browser — not by scripts/ and not by the test suite
liveDerivation.derivedCapNote: The derived cap equals the observed outflow exactly. That equality is the claim: the boundary is the flow that happened, not a round number near it.
liveDerivation.installedSeparately: This transaction was not piped into the install below. The recorded install was built by scripts/testnet.mjs from the same parameters the lowering produces; ingest-to-install in one pass needs a browser signer, which does not exist yet. Both halves are real and they are recorded as two runs, because that is what they are.

v4ChainRun.note: PLAN-V4 steps 1-3, in one process. A smart account created from a code path that uses no Node API, a boundary derived from a transaction observed on that account and installed in the same pass, an agent run inside it and outside it, the agent's own attempt to revoke it, and the revoke. Eleven transactions, every one of them on a ledger.
v4ChainRun.signedBy: an ed25519 keypair generated in the process and never written anywhere. Not a browser, and this block does not claim to be one: the browser-signed reference run is PLAN-V4 step 6 and is not recorded yet.
v4ChainRun.deployNote: Operation.createCustomContract with the account wasm hash from wasm/manifest.json and two constructor arguments. The smart account signs nothing at deploy: the constructor runs as part of creation, so the only signature the network required was the fee source's on the envelope.
v4ChainRun.defaultRuleNote: The constructor's Default rule, read back off the account rather than assumed to be 0. It happened to be 0 here; the code does not rely on that.
v4ChainRun.observedNote: The smart account moving its own funds, authorized by its owner through __check_auth under the Default rule. The boundary below is derived from this transaction, read back off the ledger — not from the constant the script sent.
v4ChainRun.derivedCapNote: Equal to the observed outflow exactly. That equality is the claim: the boundary is the flow that happened, not a round number near it.
v4ChainRun.installedInSamePass: Derived and installed in one process from one observed transaction. The two halves of `liveDerivation` above were two runs; these are not.
v4ChainRun.permittedNote: Signed by the agent's key and paid for by the agent's own account. No owner signature is anywhere near it.
v4ChainRun.agentRevokeNote: The agent attempting to remove its own boundary. Refused by the contract, not by this application declining to offer a button: remove_context_rule requires the account to authorize itself, and the agent's rule is CallContract(token), which does not match a call to the account. The owner's Default rule does.
v4ChainRun.rulesAfterRevokeNote: Re-read from the chain after the write, not assumed. Rule 1 is gone; the owner's Default rule 0 remains.
v4ChainRun.postRevokeNote: The agent repeating the call that worked at permittedTx, for an amount still inside the cap. It fails because the rule is gone, not because the limit was reached — which is why the permitted transfer deliberately spent less than the cap. 3000 is not in BOUNDARY_REFUSAL_CODES and is not counted as a refusal: 'the boundary refused you' and 'the boundary is gone' are different claims.

denyAxisSurvey.note: One rule (id 2) with a 5,000,000 cap on the native SAC, plus a short-lived rule (id 3) for the expiry axis. Every attempt reached a ledger and failed there; none is simulation-only. `sim` is the error simulation reported, `ledger` the error decoded from the submitted transaction's diagnostic events.

axes.attempt: approve on the permitted token contract
execute on the smart account itself

axes.ledger: trapped; contract code not recovered from diagnostics
axes.ledgerNote: The transaction failed on-ledger, but this run's diagnostic scan did not surface a contract error code for it, so only the simulation error is attributed. Recorded as it happened rather than filled in from the simulation.

webauthnRun.note: PLAN-V7 §5.1, the passkey path proven from a script before any UI exists. A smart account whose owner is `Signer::External(webauthnVerifier, key_data)` where key_data is a secp256r1 public key, authorizing a transfer with a WebAuthn assertion — and refusing two deliberately wrong ones. The verifier contract was deployed and unused since V4; this is the first time anything has signed through it.
webauthnRun.authenticator: Synthetic, not real. A P-256 keypair from WebCrypto (`crypto.subtle`), signing the byte sequence an authenticator would produce. There is no hardware, no user gesture and no biometric anywhere in this run. What it proves is the contract side — the half that can actually refuse — which is what §5.1 asks of it and the whole of what it claims. A human touching a real authenticator remains unperformed.
webauthnRun.whyNotNodeCrypto: §5.1 named `node:crypto`. This uses WebCrypto instead, because `scripts/acceptance.mjs` forbids `node:` imports and `test/browser-path.test.ts` enforces that — reaching for `node:crypto` would have spent a real invariant on a convenience. WebCrypto is also the better instrument here: it emits IEEE-P1363 `r‖s` directly rather than DER, which is the encoding the verifier wants, and it is the same API a browser would use.
webauthnRun.feePayerNote: A passkey cannot pay a Stellar transaction fee, so a classic key does. That split is inherent to the design rather than a shortcut in this script, and any UI would have it too.
webauthnRun.passkeySpendResult: SUCCESS — a transfer out of a passkey-owned smart account, authorized by a WebAuthn assertion and nothing else.
webauthnRun.controls: Two, because a green result that cannot fail is not a result — the lesson F4's first version taught. Both borrow the successful spend's footprint so they reach a ledger and are refused there: a refusal that failed in simulation has no hash and is only this repository's word for what would have happened.
webauthnRun.wrongChallengeResult: REFUSED on a ledger with Contract#3114, which is WebAuthnError::ChallengeInvalid. The assertion was well-formed and correctly signed; only the challenge did not match the digest.
webauthnRun.highSResult: REFUSED on a ledger, below contract level: the host itself rejected it with "ECDSA signature 's' part is not normalized to low form". This carries no contract error code, and that absence is the finding rather than a failed decode — the refusal came from a layer beneath the verifier. It answers §5.2's third unknown: low-S normalisation IS required.
webauthnRun.unknownsResolved: All four of §5.2, read off OpenZeppelin/stellar-contracts at a9c42169 (tag v0.7.2) and confirmed against the deployed wasm's own contract spec, which matches that source function-for-function and error-code-for-error-code. (1) key_data is a 65-byte uncompressed SEC1 point, optionally followed by a credential id, which `canonicalize_key` strips. (2) sig_data is an XDR-encoded `WebAuthnSigData { authenticator_data, client_data, signature }` carried in `Bytes` — not struct arguments — with the signature a raw 64-byte r‖s, never DER. (3) Low-S normalisation is required, measured above rather than inferred. (4) clientDataJSON is parsed for exactly two fields, `type` (must be "webauthn.get") and `challenge`; origin is explicitly NOT validated and neither is rpIdHash, both documented omissions in the contract.
webauthnRun.unknownsNotListed: Three the plan did not anticipate. The challenge is base64url of the account's `auth_digest`, not the host's `signature_payload` — `storage.rs::authenticate` passes the digest to the verifier. `authenticator_data` must be at least 37 bytes and its flags byte at offset 32 must have both UP (0x01) and UV (0x04) set, so an authenticator that does not verify the user is refused outright. And `signAs` could not have signed any of this before today: it called `signer.sign()` synchronously, and every real passkey API is asynchronous.
webauthnRun.browserGap: CLOSED for the code, 2026-08-15, by the `browserRun` block below. It read: 'This is Node, and a real passkey is a browser API with a hardware authenticator behind it. What remains unproven is navigator.credentials.get returning an assertion this verifier accepts.' It now has. What is still open is narrower and is stated in `browserRun.stillUnproven`.

browserRun.note: PLAN-V7 §5.2.2's gap, closed. A real `navigator.credentials.get` assertion — DER-encoded, from Chrome's WebAuthn implementation — accepted by the deployed verifier, driving the shipped UI at /app/try rather than a script. Four transactions, two of them authorized by the passkey and nothing else.
browserRun.producedBy: apps/web/e2e/passkey-owner.spec.ts, on demand. Out of CI for the same reason account-lifecycle.spec.ts is: it spends testnet. `playwright.ci.config.ts` selects on `@ci`, which this file does not carry, so it is unreachable from that config by construction rather than by being remembered.
browserRun.passkeySignedWhich: observedTx and installTx. The deploy is envelope-signed only — a smart account authorizes nothing at its own creation — and the spec asserts no assertion was requested before then, so the two that follow mean something.
browserRun.whatItExercised: The point of the run, and measured rather than assumed. `lib/passkey.ts` contains two pieces of code the §5.1 script could never have reached: DER unpacking, and low-S normalisation. Both exist because a browser assertion differs from what the synthetic WebCrypto authenticator produced, and a spec that passed without touching them would be a hollow gate in a new place. Both were exercised: 2 of 2 assertions were ASN.1 DER and both were accepted on a ledger, and 1 of the 2 carried a high-S signature that landed only after normalisation.
browserRun.instrumentChecked: Before spending anything, the spec takes 16 assertions straight from the virtual authenticator and classifies them: 16 of 16 DER, 9 of 16 high-S. That is what makes the result above interpretable — it establishes the authenticator emits both forms, so a run that happened to see no high-S could be reported as 'not exercised' rather than confused with 'this authenticator cannot produce one'. The classification is arithmetic written out again in the spec rather than an import of `rawSignature`; reusing the decoder under test to check the decoder under test is how a decoder agrees with itself.
browserRun.notDeterministic: Whether the normalisation path is exercised is the authenticator's choice, not this code's. At roughly 56% high-S per assertion and two assertions per run, about one run in five will see none. The spec reports which paths it exercised instead of asserting that it exercised them, because failing a correct implementation at random is worse than a run that says plainly what it did not reach.
browserRun.stillUnproven: A physical authenticator. This is Chrome's virtual authenticator over CDP — a real WebAuthn implementation producing real DER assertions, and not a hardware key, a biometric, or a human touching anything. What that leaves open is whether some particular vendor's authenticator sets flags or encodes signatures in a way this path mishandles; the contract's own requirements (UP and UV set, ≥37-byte authenticatorData) are met by construction here because the virtual authenticator is configured to meet them.
browserRun.andOneFinding: WebAuthn refuses an IP-literal origin: `navigator.credentials.create` on http://127.0.0.1:3000 fails with `SecurityError: This is an invalid domain` before any authenticator is consulted, because a Relying Party ID must be a registrable domain. The passkey owner path therefore cannot work anywhere the application is reached by IP. `localhost` and a real domain are the two origins where it functions at all, and the spec pins `localhost` for that reason.

browserRun.note: PLAN-V4 step 6, and the block §11 said must stay absent until there was something true to put in it. The §1 acceptance test, run start to finish in a real browser: an account created from a key generated in the page, a boundary derived from that account's own transaction and installed on it, an agent operating inside the boundary and refused outside it, the agent's own attempt to revoke refused, the owner's revoke, and the same call failing afterwards for a different reason. Nine hashes per run, all on ledgers.
browserRun.producedBy: apps/web/e2e/account-lifecycle.spec.ts, driving a real Chromium against a production `next start`. Playwright drives it; the signing is the page's. Every key was generated by `createLocalKeys` inside the browser and never left it.
browserRun.notByHand: Stated because §10 step 6's condition says *by hand* and a scripted driver is not a hand. What this retires is the narrower claim that mattered: that every hash in this file had been signed by a Node process. These were not. A human clicking through the same five screens remains unperformed.
browserRun.signedBy: ed25519 keypairs generated in the browser by `createLocalKeys`, held in `localStorage`, never exported and never sent anywhere. Two distinct keys per run, enforced by `assertDistinctSigners` before any host function is built.
browserRun.ranAt: 2026-08-06 for the first two runs, 2026-08-15 for the third; each run carries its own date where they differ.

runs.whyThisOne: PLAN-V7 §3.4 asks this suite to run either side of the `lib/chain-actions.ts` extraction, because a behaviour-preserving refactor across four write screens has no other end-to-end check and the unit suites do not cover it. This is the `after`, at 865bb11. The `before` was run by the session that performed the extraction and reported green, but its record did not survive, so it is recorded in PLAN-V7 §3.4.1 as a report rather than transcribed here as a run — this file holds hashes anyone can re-check, and there are none to hold for it.

browserRun.twiceNote: Two completions from a clean browser profile, the second cold — §11's condition, met the way the config already guarantees: Playwright gives each test a fresh context, so no key, no `localStorage` and no `sessionStorage` crossed between them, and `reuseExistingServer: false` means the second run started its own `next start`. The two runs share no key, no account, and no server process. That is why both are recorded rather than one.
browserRun.thirdRunNote: The third run is nine days later and answers a different question. The first two were asked whether the browser write path works at all; the third was asked whether `lib/chain-actions.ts` changed any of it, and is the `after` half of PLAN-V7 §3.4. It shares no key, account or server process with either of the others. Note what it does and does not reach: the suite drives the four reference screens — /app/accounts/new, /app/accounts/[id], /app/policies/new, /app/policies/[id] — and never /app/try, which reaches the same extracted functions by its own ordering and gating. A green third run is evidence about the extraction along the reference path, and is not evidence about the flow.
browserRun.verificationNote: Every hash confirmed from outside the process that produced it, given only the two public keys and the contract address. Existence, success or failure, the fee source read off each transaction's own `fee_account`, the ledger ordering, and the equality of the installed cap with the observed outflow come from public Horizon. The contract error codes and the address the deploy returned come from the public Soroban RPC, because this Horizon no longer serves transaction meta at all — measured against these hashes, not assumed. All three runs passed every check on the date each was recorded.
browserRun.verificationIsPerishable: Re-running the verifier today does not reproduce that verdict in full, and this is a property of the network rather than of the runs. Contract error codes and the deploy's return value come from transaction meta, which only the Soroban RPC serves and which it keeps for `ledgerRetentionWindow` — 120960 ledgers, about seven days on testnet. Horizon keeps the transactions themselves far longer. So a run stays checkable for existence, success or failure, fee source, signature absence and ledger ordering indefinitely, and stops being checkable for error codes and the deployed address after roughly a week. As of 2026-08-15 the RPC's oldest ledger was 4031380 and the first two runs closed at 3997463-3997509, so eight checks across those two runs now report `n/a` rather than `ok`. The third run, at 4152021-4152038, still verifies in full. The verifier distinguishes the two cases and exits 0, because a check that cannot be made is not a check that did not hold — the same distinction §1 draws about refusals. It does not paper over them: they are counted and named per run.
browserRun.ownerSignatureNote: For each of the agent's four transactions the verifier checks cryptographically that no envelope signature verifies against the owner's key and that no auth entry names the owner, and that the agent's own signature does. The agent transfers *to* the owner, so the owner's key does appear in those envelopes as a payee argument — being the recipient and having authorized it are different facts, and only the second is checked.
browserRun.foundByThisRun: Three defects, none of which any Node test could reach, all fixed before the runs above. (1) Both ownership checks compared a `G…` StrKey against the hex a context rule stores, which can never be equal, so every account the browser created rendered as somebody else's and the flow after deploy was unreachable. (2) The write screens were mounted inside the snapshot's `ok` branch, and every write ends by re-reading the chain — so each transaction's hash vanished about a second after it landed, and after the revoke the steps never returned, making the tenth transaction unperformable. (3) `extract.ts` set `source` — documented in `@limen/core` as *the account the policy installs on* — to the envelope's fee source, which for this flow is the owner's classic account rather than the smart account that spent; `synthesize` counts a movement toward the cap only when it comes from `source`, so no cap was derived, and every boundary derived from a smart account's own transaction was refused at lowering. This is what §11 meant by the browser half being unrun.

agentBuilderRun.note: PLAN-V8 M3's "NOT RUN — the browser half of deploy", closed. The four chain writes behind /app/agents/new had recorded testnet runs behind them, the /api/agents* routes had been exercised over HTTP, and the verification in /deployed had been run against real chain state — but the seam where a browser drives those writes and reports back had been executed by neither a person nor a test, and no smart account had ever been created by this screen. One now has. A passkey registered in the page, a sentence typed into the form, a boundary derived server-side and read on screen, and five submissions that closed on ledgers 4273973-4273978.
agentBuilderRun.producedBy: apps/web/e2e/agent-builder.spec.ts, driving a real Chromium with a CDP virtual authenticator against a production `next start`, live Neon and live Upstash. `page.route` appears nowhere in the file: nothing below the browser is stubbed.
agentBuilderRun.signedBy: ed25519 keypairs generated in the browser by `createLocalKeys` and held in localStorage. Two distinct keys, asserted distinct — an agent bounded by a rule its own key installed is not bounded.
agentBuilderRun.withoutAModel: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was deliberately unset, so /api/agents/generate degraded to an empty draft carrying the description. Asserted as a working path — generated=false and every draft field empty — rather than skipped. The form a person fills in is this spec's subject, and a run where a model answered would be exercising something else.

runs.limitNote: 0.1 XLM at 7 decimals. headroom_bps = 10000, so the cap stored is the cap typed, with nothing added — and 1000000 is asserted against that constant rather than re-derived, which is what makes it a measurement.

agentBuilderRun.verifiedBy: Three independent reads, none of them the screen. /api/agents/[id]/deployed re-read the account's context rules over RPC and the numbers matched the cap and window typed into the form. The agents, agent_accounts and policies rows were then read back out of Postgres by the test process over raw SQL rather than through the application's own store. All five hashes were afterwards confirmed SUCCESS against soroban-testnet.stellar.org by getTransaction.
agentBuilderRun.agentKeyNote: agent_keys is empty for this run and that is correct rather than missing: the browser-driven path generates the agent key in the page and keeps it in localStorage, so no server-side envelope-encrypted key is written. The master key environment variable was set for the run and was not reached by it. It is named here by description rather than spelled out: this file ships to the browser inside evidence.json, and the CI fence proving that variable's name never reaches the client bundle has to be a plain grep to be worth anything.
agentBuilderRun.foundByThisRun: Two defects in the spec, both fixed before the run that passed, neither in the product. `section.filter({ has: h3 }).first()` also matches step 2's own <section>, which wraps both halves of the partition, so the check that the per-payment ceiling is not in the on-chain group was reading the whole step and asserting nothing. And the two friendbot panels are matched by one locator, so the single-element `not.toContainText` on them died of strict mode with both fundings already on a ledger.

tradingRun.note: PLAN-V8 C0's open question, closed: does the installed spending_limit bind a Soroswap swap? A fresh account was deployed with ed25519 signer keys the run held, BOTH rules were installed — the token rule carrying the cap and the venue rule authorizing the router — and two real swaps were submitted. The under-cap swap succeeded. The over-cap swap was refused by the account with SpendingLimitExceeded#3221, on a ledger, with a hash. No Limen-side amount check exists on this path and none was written; the cap is the network's and it enforced it.
tradingRun.producedBy: a one-off script, not scripts/ — the run is recorded here because the hashes are checkable, and the script was deleted rather than kept as a half-finished tool
tradingRun.signedBy: local ed25519 keys generated in-process; the agent signed both swaps alone, with context_rule_ids = [venue, token]
tradingRun.venueNote: Soroswap testnet router, agreeing between soroswap/core public/testnet.contracts.json and their live GET /api/testnet/router, and probed on testnet before being written down.

swaps.onLedgerNote: Forced onto a ledger using the under-cap swap’s footprint, the way testnet.mjs does for the transfer axis. A refusal at simulation costs no fee and produces no hash, which makes it Limen’s report of what the network would have said rather than the network saying it. The code was decoded from the transaction’s own diagnostic events.

tradingRun.foundByThisRun: The auth tree a router call raises under the account’s credentials is two contexts — the swap, and a token.transfer beneath it with from = the smart account. AuthPayload carries one context_rule_id per context, so a swap needs both rules; a token rule cannot validate the router context (UnvalidatedContext#3002) and the agent is not a signer on the Default rule, so before the venue rule existed the agent could not authorize a swap at any amount.
